name: Cut-resistant gloves
summary: Knitted gloves of tough fibres such as HPPE, para-aramid or steel blends, often with a rubbery palm coating, rated to slow a slicing cut.
uses: Sheet metal, broken glass, knives and cut wire: lowers the chance and depth of a slicing cut. No glove is cut-proof (SUPERIOR CUT, MCR CUT LEVELS)
Cut-resistant is not puncture-resistant (MECHANIX PUNCTURE); needles get through knit gloves not rated for them (ISHN NEEDLES); no glove is puncture-proof (MCR CUT LEVELS)
The rating covers the palm unless the maker says more; backs and fingertips may be weaker (SUPERIOR CUT)

Never at drill presses, lathes, mills, band saws, bench grinders, slicers or rollers, or near any shaft or belt that could pull a glove in: a caught glove drags the hand in (OSHA 3170, CCOHS DRILL PRESS, CCOHS METALWORKING, OSHA BAND SAW)
A grip coating adds grip, not cut resistance (SUPERIOR CUT); heat or chemical protection needs its own marking, such as EN 407 or EN 374 (HSE GLOVES)
Hand-held grinders and winch rope are the exceptions: CCOHS names tight-fitting gloves for grinder attachments and Warn heavy leather gloves for winch rope (CCOHS GRINDER ATTACHMENTS, WARN RIGGING)
identify: Usually a knitted shell of HPPE, para-aramid or blends with metal, often with a coated palm; butchers use steel chainmail (SUPERIOR CUT). US: ANSI/ISEA 105 cut level A1 to A9, the load in grams a blade needs to cut through on the TDM test (ASTM F2992): A1 200, A2 500, A3 1,000, A4 1,500, A5 2,200, A6 3,000, A7 4,000, A8 5,000, A9 6,000 g or more (MCR CUT LEVELS for the 2016 edition; MCR ANSI 105-2024). HexArmor calls the 2024 revision mainly a labelling change (HEXARMOR 105-2024). The 2024 edition shows cut, puncture (0 to 5) and abrasion on one pentagon badge, with X for not tested (MCR ANSI 105-2024, HEXARMOR 105-2024). Europe: the EN 388 shield with digits for abrasion (0 to 4), coup cut (0 to 5, or X when the glove dulls the blade so the coup test doesn't apply), tear (0 to 4) and puncture (0 to 4), then an EN ISO 13997 (TDM) cut letter A to F (2, 5, 10, 15, 22, 30 newtons), then P if it passed impact (EJENDALS EN 388). So 4X43D reads: abrasion 4, coup not valid, tear 4, puncture 3, TDM D. The coup number and the TDM letter don't convert to each other: the standard says the two methods don't correlate (EJENDALS EN 388). Needle protection is a separate test with a fine needle (MECHANIX PUNCTURE).
test: There is no field test for the cut level, so the printed rating is all you have, and it only counts on a glove in good condition. Reject gloves with holes, cut or broken yarns, palms or fingertips worn thin, or a coating peeling off: a gap in the knit has no protection at all. The rating comes from a lab test of a blade drawn across the palm material (SUPERIOR CUT, MCR CUT LEVELS). No glove is cut-proof, even chainmail can be cut with enough effort (SUPERIOR CUT), and a cut rating says nothing about puncture (MECHANIX PUNCTURE). Fit: snug so you can grip and feel, without folds that catch (HSE GLOVES). Before work at a drill press, lathe, mill, band saw, bench grinder or roller, take them off: gloves caught in drill bits, rollers and slicer blades have pulled hands in and cost fingers (OSHA 3170), and CCOHS says not to wear gloves at a drill press or near rotating blades (CCOHS DRILL PRESS, CCOHS WOODWORKING). Handle glass and sheet by the edges you have filed or taped, and keep the gloved hand out of the line of the cut.

decay.note: Estimate. The only maker figure found is a nominal 5 years for synthetic coatings such as nitrile and urethane, kept away from heat, ozone and UV (S+H SHELF LIFE); it says nothing of knit shells. Worn gloves fail first.

improvise: Better than nothing: thick leather work gloves protect against blows, chips and rough objects (OSHA 3151), but leather is not inherently cut-resistant (SUPERIOR CUT), so don't trust it against a drawn blade. Not enough against sharp edges: fabric gloves don't give sufficient protection for rough, sharp or heavy material (OSHA 3151), and sharp objects can puncture disposable gloves, needles included (FDA GLOVES, ISHN NEEDLES). Work so a slip can't reach you: file or tape cut edges as you make them, cut away from your body, clamp the work instead of holding it, and lift broken glass with a dustpan, pliers or thick folded cardboard. Never reach blind into bins, cushions or cavities. At a drill press, lathe, mill, band saw, bench grinder or roller, go bare-handed and keep your hands clear: no glove is safer there (OSHA 3170, CCOHS DRILL PRESS). A cut glove is not a needle glove: needles get through knit gloves not rated for them (ISHN NEEDLES), and a needle glove is labelled separately (MECHANIX PUNCTURE). For needles and syringes, use pliers or tongs and a hard container, not your hands.

buildings.loc: Glove rack in the work-wear aisle or by the checkout
PPE crib or vending machine, sheet metal and glass handling stations
Site trailer and trade gang boxes (glaziers, HVAC, sheet metal)
Shipping and receiving, near box cutters and strapping tools
Meat room and deli: cut or chainmail gloves by slicers and bandsaws
Office supply shelf and dismantling bays
Kitchen drawer by the mandoline, slicer or oyster knives
Glove box on the parts counter or toolboxes
